Its resonator gives the sound a marked metal resonance, producing a brilliant tone something like a brass instrument. The range is wide, from a warm bass to a clear treble, but the upper middle is the most prominent. Against a traditional acoustic guitar the resonator guitar is louder and sharper, and it is not easily buried in a band. Its way of resonating is unusual: the vibration of the metal cone amplifies the sound wave, which gives the instrument a particular quiver and a mechanical feel. This tone suits bluegrass, country and folk styles especially well, and can create a nostalgic, rooted atmosphere.

It was designed in the first place to compete in volume with brass and percussion in dance bands, and later, because its tone is so distinctive, it came to be used in bluegrass and the blues. There are two ways of playing it, square-neck and round-neck: the square neck is usually laid flat across the lap and stopped with a steel bar, while the round neck can be held like a conventional guitar or played lap-style, and blues players often use a bottleneck slide.

Later, because its tone is so distinctive, it stayed in use in bluegrass and the blues. Bluegrass tradition mostly uses the square-neck resonator guitar, played lap-style; the blues prefers the round neck, usually with a bottleneck slide.

When it sounds, the vibration of the strings passes through the bridge to the metal cone rather than to the top. The square neck can be played only lap-style with a steel bar, always with high string action and an open tuning. The round neck can be played lap-style or in the Spanish guitar position; the action can be set from half an inch, which suits a slide, down to an ordinary fretting height, and a compromise setting that lets the upper strings be played with a bottleneck while the rest are still fretted is common. In bluegrass the square neck is used more, in the blues the round neck.
諧振吉他起源於1920年代北美，為在舞蹈樂團中取得更大音量而發展。1927年，J: The resonator guitar originated in North America in the 1920s, developed to get more volume in dance bands. In 1927 John Dopyera and George Beauchamp founded the National String Instrument Corporation and began production with a metal body and three cones; in 1928 Dopyera and his brothers formed a separate company, Dobro, which used a single reverse cone and a spider bridge, giving more volume at lower cost. In 1932 the Dopyera brothers merged the two companies, and in 1941 production stopped when the United States entered the war. After the war it was carried on by Emile and Rudy Dopyera and by brands such as Gibson, and it spread to Brazil, Australia, Czechoslovakia, Asia and South Africa, so that several makers now produce it.
